top_choice_rationale: Mircea Cărtărescu (P002) remains my first choice, though by a narrow margin. I apply one standard to every candidate: a recognisable voice that keeps developing, and seriousness of imaginative purpose. His project runs from the early poetry through the Blinding trilogy to Solenoid. In it, memory, the body and dream are built into the structure and the sentences, not laid over a plot. I read the digressions as method, an accumulating inner cosmos. That reading rests on public knowledge and translation, not on verified Romanian reading, and I cannot confirm that the late novels develop rather than repeat. Anne Carson (P001) is a close second. A citation anchored in her original poetry, verse narrative, elegy and essays (Autobiography of Red, Nox, The Beauty of the Husband, Eros the Bittersweet) is workable. The remaining risks are possible mannerism after roughly 2010, a case resting on a stable core of books, and dependence on layout and book design. I weigh these as risks, not established defects. The gap between the two is small and is a matter of weighting, not talent. Four colleagues' support for Carson is not evidence of literary merit. Either writer ranks well above no award, since both candidates show distinctive voice, formal achievement and imaginative depth, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. The profile records no personal, professional or family tie to Cărtărescu, Carson or any other shortlisted writer. For disclosure only, my own fiction and criticism on Central Europe and my long residence in Prague and Vienna are the same wider region Cărtărescu writes from. That is context, not a connection or evidence of preference, and I do not adjudicate it.
